title: Bidirectional Dijkstra in Reykjavík: Faster Routes!
description: Watch Bidirectional Dijkstra race from both ends to find the shortest path across a mapped street graph in Reykjavík’s downtown grid. The visualization highlights how meeting in the middle reduces explored nodes while still guaranteeing optimality.
ig_caption:
❄️🗺️ Reykjavík feels like a maze—so let’s solve it the smart way with **Bidirectional Dijkstra**!

🔁 **How it works (deep + practical):**
Instead of running Dijkstra from just the start, we launch **two coordinated searches**:
- one forward from the source
- one backward from the destination (on the reversed graph)

⚡ Each side expands the lowest-cost frontier (priority queue by tentative distance), and when the searches **meet** at a common node, we can compute the best candidate path length and stop early once no cheaper route is possible. ✅

🧠 **Graph theory in real street maps:**
Your road network becomes a **weighted graph** (intersections = nodes, streets = edges). Edge weights can represent distance, travel time, or even penalties (turn costs, slopes, traffic factors). Bidirectional Dijkstra exploits the structure of the graph to cut down the number of explored nodes while preserving the **optimal shortest path guarantee**.

🎥 Watch the expanding waves converge in the visualization—this is why “meet-in-the-middle” is a big deal for shortest-path routing.

fb_caption:
🚗💡 In this pathfinding visualization from Reykjavík (Miðborg), **Bidirectional Dijkstra** searches from *both* the start and destination on a weighted street-graph. By meeting in the middle, it often explores far fewer intersections than standard Dijkstra—while still guaranteeing the shortest route.

📌 Graph search basics: roads become edges, intersections become nodes, and the algorithm uses priority queues to expand the cheapest frontier first.
